articles.title: NATO 3.0 and the Long Road to a European Pillar - Defense.info
articles.summary: NATO 3.0 and the Long Road to a European Pillar  Defense.info
articles.full_text:
On September 16, 2026, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte delivered the Ditchley Foundation’s 62nd Annual Lecture at Ditchley Park in Oxfordshire. In the house where Churchill once met Roosevelt’s envoys to make the case for Lend-Lease, Rutte set out what he calls “NATO 3.0”: “not a reboot, but a rebalancing of our security for the better,” or, in his own summary phrase, “a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO.”
One line in the speech matters most to me: “To stay transatlantic, NATO is becoming more European.”
I have spent four decades working on that proposition. In 1991 I published The Europeanization of the Alliance, which grew out of interviews across Paris, Bonn, London and Brussels in the late 1980s. Its argument was that the Alliance’s future depended on building a European pillar inside it, not outside it or against it. To hear the Secretary General make that case at Ditchley as official Alliance policy is to be reminded how long the idea took to arrive, and how much had to go wrong before it did.
That is the subject of my forthcoming book, The Western Alliance in Transition: From the Cold War’s End to the Battle for Europe’s Future, the first volume in a four-volume series on the Alliance. Reading Rutte’s speech against the book is instructive.
The speech describes the destination. The book explains the route, and why the journey took so long.
Three Eras, or Five Phases?
Rutte tells NATO’s history in three eras. NATO 1.0 “stood its ground, held the line, and pushed back against the brute force of the Soviet Union.” NATO 2.0 “started at this ‘end of history,'” and was “marked by the move away from the territorial defence of Europe to ‘out of area’ operations,” while “defence budgets declined, and military power dwindled across Europe.” NATO 3.0 is the correction.
As a summary for a lecture, it works.
But Rutte’s NATO 2.0 spans three distinct periods, each with its own logic, and the differences matter.
The first is what I call the structural transformation decade, 1990 to 2001. It was not a pause while the end of history played itself out. It was a period of high-stakes decisions made under real uncertainty, built on three bets: that Russia could be integrated into a cooperative European security framework; that consolidating Soviet nuclear weapons under Moscow’s control would be stabilizing; and that NATO enlargement could proceed without foreclosing the first two. None of these bets was irrational at the time. Each had its own logic, and each its own way of failing.
The second is the expeditionary detour, from 2001 to 2014. After 9/11 the Alliance remade itself as a reservoir of forces for U.S.-led coalitions in Afghanistan, Iraq and Libya. Those operations produced real achievements in deployability and multinational command. They also hollowed out the core mission. Heavy forces shrank, air defenses aged, and the analytical community that should have been tracking Russian military modernization was allowed to atrophy. By 2014 NATO was, as I put it in the book, “institutionally intact but strategically hollow with respect to the one mission its founding treaty was written to perform.”
The third is the partial return to direct defense after Crimea, from 2014 to 2021. The Alliance recognized the problem but could not close the gap between political commitment and military means. Thin stockpiles, fragile supply chains and fragmented procurement limited what governments could do, even once they understood what needed doing.
Then came the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which turned that gap from a seminar topic into a question of survival. What Rutte calls NATO 3.0 grew out of that experience.
The distinction is not academic. If NATO 2.0 was simply an era of complacency, then NATO 3.0 is a recovery of nerve. If it was a sequence of reasonable bets, a costly detour and an incomplete recovery, then NATO 3.0 is something harder: a reckoning with structural tensions the Alliance has managed and deferred, but never resolved.
Where the Speech and the Book Converge
On the substance of what has changed, the speech and the book line up closely.
The burden. Rutte rejects “the casual assumption, made by many, that our biggest friend and Ally would always provide most of the muscle and pick up the bill, no matter what.” The book traces that assumption back further, to the Atlanticized template of American primacy and European dependency set during the Cold War and repeated after 2001, when Washington chose to fight in Afghanistan largely on its own terms, taking allied support selectively.
The geography. Rutte notes that eight of NATO’s nine Forward Land Forces, “from the Black Sea to the Arctic Circle,” are led by European Allies or Canada. In the book I argue that Finland and Sweden’s accession fused the Baltic, Nordic and Arctic theaters into a single strategic space, and that the states closest to Russia have become agenda-setters for the Alliance. Europeanization has not disappeared; it has been redistributed north and east. The resulting structure is arguably more serious militarily than the Franco-German framework it is replacing.
Industry. “Military might and industrial might go hand in hand,” Rutte said. As I read it, that is the central lesson of the Ukraine war. Deterrence now rests as much on factories, power grids, data networks, ports and rail corridors as on brigades and battlegroups. An alliance that cannot move forces across its territory, protect its energy and digital systems, or replace what it uses up in war has not been transformed, whatever its communiqués say.
Ukraine as teacher. Rutte said that “what we are learning from Ukraine is helping strengthen our own defences, including with Ukraine’s expertise in drones and air defence.” Ukraine’s wartime industrial adaptation has made it both partner and teacher for the West, a reversal few in Western capitals expected in 2022.
Plural leadership. Speaking in Britain, Rutte stressed the UK’s role, from the Coalition of the Willing to the deep precision strike initiative and the sharing of Storm Shadow technology with Ukraine. That fits what the book describes as a more plural leadership in European defense: Anglo-French activism, German industrial weight, Polish strategic scale, Nordic seriousness and Baltic urgency. Strategic direction is shared rather than centrally commanded. That may make the system more resilient, but it also means political coherence has to be built continuously.
Integration. Rutte said NATO must be “the engine for this change – turning national investment into common requirements, integrated forces, credible plans, and collective deterrent power.” The least glamorous part of that engine is standardization: the more than 1,300 standardization agreements and allied publications that let thirty-two militaries fight as one force. It rarely makes headlines, but it is what turns political commitment into military capability.
Where the Speech Leaves Questions Open
There are also places where the speech is quieter than the history suggests it should be.
The Russia question. Rutte described Russia’s hybrid campaign against the Alliance as “a sign of weakness, and a symptom of Putin’s failure in Ukraine.” That may be so. But the long effort to integrate Russia, through Partnership for Peace, the NATO–Russia Council and successive resets, failed, and nothing stable has replaced it. The Alliance has found a more credible deterrence posture. It has not found a durable peace. NATO 3.0 answers the military problem Russia poses, not the political question of what European order follows the war.
The European Union. The speech barely mentions the EU, yet the war has shown how much military credibility depends on tools outside NATO’s mandate: industrial policy, energy security, investment screening, infrastructure protection and supply-chain resilience. These are largely EU domains. A more European NATO without a more capable, more strategic EU will reach its limits quickly. The real task is to make the layered system of NATO, the EU and coalitions of the willing work as a system rather than as overlapping bureaucracies.
Political will. The spending figures are striking: a commitment made at The Hague in 2025 to invest 5% of GDP in defense and security by 2035, and, by Rutte’s count, $258 billion in additional investment by European Allies and Canada across 2025 and 2026. But the lesson of the past four decades is that political will in a democratic alliance is never fixed; it must be renewed continually. The real test of NATO 3.0 is not the size of this year’s budgets but whether they are sustained after the immediate shock fades.
The American variable. Rutte was candid about the role of President Trump: “he’s right. We needed this shot of adrenaline.” That is an important admission. Washington’s pressure has driven the transformation as much as Moscow’s aggression. It also points beyond the Alliance itself, to the broader question of how political change within Western societies, the United States included, is reshaping the strategic West. That question lies outside The Western Alliance in Transition, which deliberately stops in 2025, and is the subject of a separate book I am preparing on the transformation of the West.
The transatlantic logic. One of the strongest passages in the speech deserves more attention than it is likely to get. “The Russian nuclear submarines for example coming out of the Kola Peninsula aren’t targeting Europe,” Rutte said. “Their aim in wartime is the destruction of the U.S. homeland.” This is the best answer to anyone in Washington who sees European defense as Europe’s problem alone. Defending the North Atlantic and the Arctic is defending the United States. articles.title: China shock: EU says trade deal could cut up to 50% of Chinese EV and plug-in hybrid imports - Fortune
articles.summary: China shock: EU says trade deal could cut up to 50% of Chinese EV and plug-in hybrid imports  Fortune
articles.full_text:
The top trade envoys for China and the European Union agreed Friday on a broad initial deal following two days of talks aimed at calming escalating tensions over trade imbalances, the EU trade commissioner said.
Neither side provided clear details on the preliminary deal, but European Commissioner for Trade Maros Sefcovic said it includes lower tariffs for some European goods to China as well as measures to stabilize rare earth supply chains.
The EU trade envoy said the deal could cut up to 50% of Chinese electric and plug-in hybrid vehicle imports to the EU and could lower tariffs on products benefiting “almost every” EU nation. The deal would require approval from leaders across the 27-nation EU.
He said that “by this step we are actually preventing several millions of car exports from China to the European Union.”
The two sides were seeking to resolve key factors behind China’s growing trade surplus, which hit 360 billion euros ($403 billion) last year.
China’s Commerce Ministry posted online that Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao expressed concerns about the EU’s recent restrictive measures. He said that China is not the root of the EU’s problems but a partner in solving them.
The head of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association, Sigrid de Vries, said that the deal appears to avert further instability in the EU and “can help facilitate the transition to a new era of Chinese presence in the European market in an orderly way and this is in the long-term interests of all parties.”
Sefcovic said he will brief EU leaders meeting in Brussels next week and seek their approval.
“They would have to see that this is convincing enough to take the other steps,” he said. “We are in a situation that they (China) could put under the threat whole sectors in the European industry, literally thousands of jobs and the public opinion and the leaders clearly expect very fast action from our side.”
Sefcovic also said both sides reached understandings to further facilitate China’s export licensing for rare earths and permanent magnets, as well as to improve access to the Chinese market for various EU products through lower most-favored-nation tariffs, including car parts, olive oil and footwear, totaling almost 4 billion euros (about $4.5 billion) in current export value.
The two sides will meet next by video in January and then in person in March.
Growing tensions
China has been pushing for the EU to stop blocking Chinese imports of advanced computer chipmaking machines, restrictions imposed on national security grounds at Washington’s behest.
Earlier, Sefcovic had said the talks this week were the culmination of three months of intensive work. He had set an October deadline for meaningful results on trade rebalancing.
Earlier in the week, the Chinese Commerce Ministry issued a statement urging the EU to avoid protectionist measures, warning that such moves could backfire.
Trade tensions have grown in recent months, with both sides imposing or considering curbs on each other’s imports.
The EU has moved to limit imports of Chinese-made electric vehicles and EV batteries and enacted measures to protect the European steel industry. It also is limiting duty-free imports of e-commerce small parcels, essentially targeting Chinese fast fashion firms.
Last week, China launched an anti-dumping investigation into imports from the EU of p-nitrotoluene, a chemical compound used in dyes and pharmaceuticals.
Chinese officials and businesses have raised concerns over reports some EU members are pushing for new measures to protect local industries.
China had a global trade surplus exceeding $1 trillion last year
Worries over surging Chinese exports to Europe and other parts of the world in what some are calling a China shock 2.0 have deepened as the U.S., especially since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to the White House, has raised tariffs and enacted other measures to try to reduce its own huge trade deficit with Beijing.
Despite the backlash from some of its trading partners, China’s global trade surplus hit $1.2 trillion in 2025 and is forecast to surpass $1 trillion again this year.
The EU’s trade deficit with China widened to 103.3 billion euros (about $116 billion) in the second quarter, as imports rose to 153.6 billion euros ($172 billion), while European exports to China climbed to 50.3 billion euros ($56 billion), according to EU statistics.
And on Wednesday, Germany blocked the sale of a major logistics firm in the port of Hamburg to the state-owned Chinese shipping behemoth Cosco over security concerns.
“As Europe’s largest economy, Germany welcomes foreign investment. At the same time, some investments can endanger the country’s security,” the German economic ministry said in a statement. “The acquisition would have deepened dependencies and jeopardized the resilience of supply chains in Germany and the EU.”

articles.summary: Ukraine war: Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 20 people  BBCStrikes killing 17 are Russia’s ‘thanks’ for US diesel sanctions lift, Zelenskyy says  POLITICO.euUkraine war briefing: Zelenskyy condemns ‘vile’ attacks from Russia that killed 20 in one apartment  The GuardianRussia Drops Deadly Bombs on Ukraine Homes After US Diesel Deal  Bloomberg.comRussia kills 20 in Ukraine as US hosts ‘productive’ talks to end war  Al Jaze...

Russia has attacked the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia with five glide bombs, killing at least 20 people including four children, local officials said.
The glide bombs hit residential buildings in the southern city on Saturday morning. At least 32 others were injured in the attack, with more still missing and believed to be under the rubble.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks on Zaporizhzhia were Russia expressing "its thanks" for a deal announced by US President Donald Trump last night easing sanctions on Moscow to import Russian diesel.
He added that 13 other regions had come under attack overnight, arguing this demonstrated Russia took "any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting".
Photos and videos from the site of one of the strikes in Zaporizhzhia show an apartment block mostly destroyed.
"The ground floor was hit, and the floors above just collapsed," acting Mayor Regina Harchenko told Ukrainian television from the scene.
She said more than 80 workers were involved in ongoing search and rescue operations which are expected to continue throughout the day.
The rescuers regularly stop to listen for any noises made by survivors who could be under the rubble.
Harchenko said Russia had struck at "our very heart" and "our littlest ones" were among those killed, adding that their deaths were "awful grief for their families. For the city."
Zaporizhzhia is a major regional centre with more than 700,000 residents. It is located less than 10 miles (16km) from the front line and is frequently attacked by Russian drones and missiles.
Zelensky was quick to criticise Trump's diesel deal with Russia, calling it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Analysts view the deal as an attempt by the US president to allay domestic concerns about high fuel prices ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.
Zelensky wrote on social media on Saturday that Russian attacks on energy facilities in the capital, Kyiv, demonstrated Russia's "true intentions".
"Russia's choice is war. And they will be ready to end it only when they feel that their ability to drag the war out is diminishing.
"Unfortunately, the signals Russia received yesterday were entirely different – signals suggesting that it could simply keep attacking. And this needs to be corrected."
Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months, as Moscow's full-scale invasion, launched in 2022, drags on.
On Thursday, at least 33 people were killed in another Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in Kramatorsk, in the eastern Donetsk region.
The day before, 22 people including five children died as a Russian missile hit an apartment block in the town of Pryluky, east of Kyiv.
The number of civilian casualties in Ukraine jumped by 55% in the first eight months of this year, according to the UN.
Russia has also stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure as winter approaches, a strategy it has undertaken in previous years. Kyiv has repeatedly accused it of targeting Ukraine's civilian population, which Moscow denies.
For its part, Ukraine has increasingly adopted a policy of striking infrastructure often deep inside Russia that is crucial to its economy, including several oil refineries and terminals.
Several strikes on data centres owned by Yandex have left the tech giant struggling to maintain services.
Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at curtailing revenue streams for Russia's war machine.

articles.summary: Ukraine takes aim at Russia’s AI data infrastructure  Al JazeeraRussian search engine Yandex struggles after Ukrainian strikes on data centres  BBCUkraine hits second major tech site, expanding range of targets inside Russia  ReutersUkraine’s drones knock out AI data center belonging to "Russia’s Google"  Ars TechnicaUkrainian drone attack takes out Russian datacenter  The Register
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian drone strikes have partly disabled an AI data centre operated by Russian digital giant Yandex.
The strike on Friday followed an attack on another of the company’s data hubs the previous day, appearing to signal that Ukraine’s military campaign is widening its scope to target Russia’s technology infrastructure. Moscow has previously targeted data hubs inside Ukraine.
Yandex, which is heavily involved in Russia’s AI development efforts, said its data centre in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow had been struck by Ukrainian drones and partly put out of action.
A day earlier, a Ukrainian attack shut down a major data hub in Sasovo in the Ryazan region, where two of the three supercomputers used to develop the company’s AI models are housed.
Yandex, which operates under close government observation, said the attacks had struck at the core of its operations and that it was trying to maintain its services.
“Our teams are working day and night to keep services running and help those affected by the incident. Right now this is our most important task, but unfortunately it is not an easy one,” it said in a statement.
The company operates numerous apps that many Russians consider essential, as well as social media networks.
Russia has struck several Ukrainian data centres and telecommunications infrastructure facilities over the past month, including targets in central Kyiv.
Damage from the attacks has forced some services to suspend operations. Roughly 100,000 households suffered temporary internet outages after an attack.
“We always respond in mirror-like fashion,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday, following the Ryazan strike. “You all know, they have been hitting and continue to hit our data centres. We are responding. I can’t share all the details.”
Missiles and energy
Kyiv also continues its campaign targeting Russia’s missile production and energy infrastructure, hoping to reduce the air strikes against which it has struggled to defend, as well as to hurt Moscow’s economic ability to wage war.
Ukraine’s military said it had hit three facilities involved in missile production across Russia overnight, including a factory in the Tver region making missile components and a centre for disassembling intercontinental ballistic missiles in the Nizhny Novgorod region.
In a statement on Telegram, the General Staff said the Russian facility for the “liquidation of intercontinental ballistic missiles” was hit to degrade Russia’s ability to source explosives and rocket fuel.
Nizhny Novgorod’s governor said that one serviceman was killed repelling the attack while drone debris caused “minimal” damage to infrastructure.
A drone attack sparked a fire at a plant in Redkino in the Tver region, but it was quickly extinguished, the local governor said.
The Ukhta oil refinery belonging to the state giant Lukoil, 1,900km (1,180 miles) from the Ukrainian border, was also struck, according to Zelenskyy.
Meanwhile, Russia’s air campaign has continued to hit civilians, despite the Kremlin’s insistence that it only attacks military targets.
Overnight strikes killed one and injured seven in the city of Zaporizhzhia, regional defence official Ivan Fedorov said on the Telegram messaging app.
Russia also struck a cargo vessel in Ukraine’s Black Sea port of Mykolaiv, the Ministry of Defence in Moscow said, according to state news agency RIA Novosti. The ministry said the vessel was being used to supply the Ukrainian military.

articles.title: Rubio says US pressure on NATO allies to boost defense spending is ‘not hostile’ - Broomfield Enterprise
articles.summary: Rubio says US pressure on NATO allies to boost defense spending is ‘not hostile’  Broomfield Enterprise
articles.full_text:
By MATTHEW LEE and BARRY HATTON
LISBON, Portugal (AP) — U.S. pressure on NATO allies to increase their defense spending “is not a hostile thing,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Thursday, but reiterated that the Trump administration wants the military alliance to be a stronger deterrent against threats.
Rubio told reporters during a visit to European NATO ally Portugal that “the stronger the members of NATO are, the stronger NATO is, the stronger the alliances and the stronger the deterrence is.”
President Donald Trump has long railed against NATO allies for spending too small a fraction of their national budgets on defense, leaving the United States to shoulder what he says is an unfair burden. Some members of the 32-country alliance have been reluctant to divert funds from other government policies, however.
“People sometimes view this call to invest more in defense as a hostile thing,” Rubio said. “It is not a hostile thing.”
Rubio, who was in Portugal on the last leg of a three-nation tour of NATO allies that also included Iceland and Greece, acknowledged that some smaller NATO members, such as Portugal, have difficulty finding the funds for major military projects.
“Every country is of a different size and proportion. Some countries can contribute more than others, but every country in NATO needs to be as strong as they can possibly be,” Rubio told a news conference in Lisbon.
He noted the danger of the war in Ukraine, following Russia’s full-scale invasion of its neighbor on Feb. 24, 2022, spilling beyond Ukrainian borders. An apparent stalemate in Ukraine could bring a military escalation in Europe, he said.
“That escalation could wind up being a sabotage campaign in neighboring countries that are members of NATO,” he said. That could “quickly turn what is a war between two countries into a much broader and far more dangerous regional conflict.”
European officials have accused Moscow of a campaign of sabotage and disruption aimed at undermining support for Ukraine and destabilizing European nations.
Rubio also said that the Trump administration will keep trying to facilitate a negotiated settlement to the war, but that it has been difficult.
“We have tried, we will continue to try, but we’re also not going to invest in pointless processes if we can’t make progress,” he said, coming after new Russian strikes in eastern Ukraine killed 30 people.
Meanwhile, Rubio also praised Portuguese efforts toward meeting the NATO target for defense spending.
Portugal, a country of fewer than 11 million people, spends just over 2% of its gross domestic product on defense, according to NATO. The government says it plans to increase defense spending to around 3%, including dual-use investments in civilian infrastructure.
That still leaves it below the 5% of GDP set aside for defense spending that Trump has demanded and that requires investment at an unprecedented scale in Europe.
Portuguese Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel said at the news conference that his country views its relationship with the U.S. as “fundamental.”
Portugal provided support for American operations in the Iran war by allowing the U.S. to use the Lajes Field air base in the mid-Atlantic Azores islands, which is strategically located for military refueling flights.
The U.S. Air Force has long had a base there under an agreement with Portugal. Unlike neighboring Spain, where Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, a Socialist, refused to allow the American military to use Spanish bases to stage operations for attacks on Iran, Portugal’s center-right government granted Washington “conditional approval” to use Lajes Field.
“Portugal is a great ally, very cooperative ally of the United States and a country with which we already have a solid and growing relationship. And we visit these countries in order to reinforce those ties,” Rubio said before arriving in Lisbon. “That’s the purpose of the trip.”
Some Portuguese political parties balked at the decision to allow the U.S. to use the Azores islands air base, however. Following a formal complaint by a small left-wing political party called Left Bloc, the country’s attorney general’s office said last week that it’s looking into whether the use of the Lajes Field base was lawful.
Rubio visited Portugal a day after delivering a speech in the Greek capital, Athens, urging European countries to save Western civilization by upholding the values and traditions of ancient Greece.

Ukrainian forces struck a Russian military training center responsible for preparing army sergeants, alongside command posts, an electronic warfare station, and multiple logistics facilities during a series of attacks on October 9 and overnight into October 10.
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on October 10, the sergeant training center was targeted near Khorly in the temporarily occupied Kherson region as part of a broader operation against Russian military infrastructure.
The strikes also hit Russian command posts near Peremozhne in the temporarily occupied Zaporizhzhia region and Dokuchaievsk in the Donetsk region.
In Russia’s Bryansk region, Ukrainian forces targeted an electronic warfare station near Trukhanove, extending the series of attacks beyond Ukrainian territory. Additional strikes focused on facilities responsible for maintaining military equipment and supplying Russian units.
Near Sukhodilsk in the temporarily occupied Luhansk region, Ukrainian forces struck a repair and recovery base used by the Russian military. Another attack targeted a fuel and lubricants depot near Chystiakove in the Donetsk region.
Two further military supply depots were hit near Rodynkove in the Donetsk region and Borovenky in the Luhansk region. According to the General Staff, the latter facility also stored engineering equipment.
The Ukrainian military did not specify the weapons used in the attacks or provide detailed information about casualties and the extent of the damage.

articles.summary: ‘So safe you could drink it’: Scientists and pesticide victims fear an EU rollback  France 24Chemical groups succeed in watering down EU pesticide rules  Financial TimesFood & Feed Omnibus, co-written by the pesticide lobby  Corporate Europe ObservatoryAgrochemical lobbyists are defending a toxic model of agriculture that is heading for collapse  EUobserverEU may abolish regular pesticide reviews — France 24  UA.NEWS
articles.full_text:
For decades, French farmers sprayed pesticides they were told were harmless. Many have since fallen ill, grappling with cancers and other diseases caused by exposure. As the EU prepares to vote on a package that would end regular safety reviews of most pesticides, victims, doctors and scientists warn it could keep harmful products on the market for longer.
For most of his life, José Nadan worked as a professional beekeeper in Morbihan, a coastal area in Brittany known for its medieval towns and fresh seafood. At the start of his career, he recalls a golden age of beekeeping, when each year, and “without much effort”, the number of hives would naturally increase.
But things took a turn for the worse in the 1980s, when the varroa mite made its way to France. A parasite, the mite weakens bees by suppressing their immune system and spreading deadly viruses that can collapse entire colonies. “We improvised trying to kill them with whatever we had until official products made their way onto the market,” Nadan recalls.
Nadan also spent many years keeping an orchard of cider apple trees he treated with a pesticide that, he was told, was organic and had no effect on humans. “The sales reps even said it was so safe you could drink it,” the 69-year-old says. “I never took the slightest precaution, spraying from my tractor as I drove along the rows of trees,” Nadan recalls. “Sometimes, because of the wind, I’d get some on my face. But I wasn’t worried.”
“I later found out it was a product like Roundup [a Monsanto weed killer] and contained glyphosate,” he says, a substance now known to be harmful to human health.
It was only after he retired that Nadan realised the consequences of being exposed to pesticides for all those years. Six years ago, he was diagnosed with prostate cancer.
His illness has officially been recognised as an occupational hazard caused by pesticides by France’s agricultural social security system.
In everything, everywhere, all at once
Pesticides are known to cause a range of health issues, including various types of cancer, respiratory diseases, neurodegenerative illnesses like Parkinson’s or Alzheimer's, cardiovascular diseases and infertility. They also impact children more than adults, leading to developmental delays and cognitive impairments.
And they are everywhere. A 2023 study in which hundreds of samples were gathered from different environments across 10 European countries found that pesticides were present in 100% of air, indoor dust and water samples.
Read morePesticides, cadmium, PFAS: France reckons with the hidden toxins in food (1/2)
Edmond Leduc, a retired doctor living close to the Belgian border in northern France, has lived next to crop fields treated with pesticides for 44 years. “The farmers working the fields practise intensive farming, so there is always a harvest,” he says. “When it’s potato season, they sometimes spray fungicides every two weeks.”
A lover of gardening, Leduc spent a lot of time outside and admits “not being very careful” in the early years. “I didn’t know the products I was inhaling were toxic.”
Leduc discovered he had lymphoma, a type of blood cancer, in 2018, and was diagnosed with prostate cancer in August of this year – two conditions linked to pesticides.
As one of Europe’s biggest agricultural producers, France is also one of its largest consumers of pesticides. And the number of requests by agricultural workers like Nadan, who are in close contact with the toxic substances, has shot up from 318 in 2024 to 975 in 2025.
Yet as the toll of pesticide exposure is becoming clearer, the EU is preparing to vote on a set of legal amendments that could make it harder to ban these harmful products.
The EU’s ‘safety lock’ at risk
Despite having a multi-layered system to assess the risk of pesticides, Europe still sees cases where they cause harm to both the environment and humans. Unlike the US, which uses a risk-based model that factors actual levels of exposure, the EU uses a hazard-based model, meaning it focuses on the inherent toxicological properties of a certain chemical before it’s approved.
But regulatory assessments are often delayed and take time, slowing down the process for pesticides to enter the market. To speed things up and cut red tape, the European Commission proposed a legislative package that would overhaul the current system. Known as Omnibus X, it would amend ten existing EU laws that cover pesticides, biocides, food residues, animal feed and official controls.
A key amendment aims to scrap the periodic re-evaluation of pesticides, which often end up causing greater damage than expected after being initially approved.
The EU ensures the move would have “no compromise on food safety or environmental protection”, but critics of the package disagree.
“New scientific findings need to be taken into account regularly, because there is always a level of uncertainty [about the risk of a pesticide] before it hits the market,” says ecotoxicologist Martina Vijver, who was up in arms when news of the package dropped. “A periodic review is a safety lock, it’s crucial, because we can’t foresee every consequence.”
An insecticide known as chlorpyrifos, for example, was approved for use in the EU back in 2006. Sprayed on crops to control pests or on grains stored in warehouses, the chemical came to be one of the most commonly used pesticides in Europe. Residues of the substance were found in fruit, vegetables, dairy products and drinking water.
When its approval came up for renewal, the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) reviewed the evidence and decided in 2019 that no safe exposure level could be set, and that chlorpyrifos didn’t meet the EU’s health requirements. Even in small doses, chlorpyrifos affects the human body’s neurological, reproductive, metabolic and immune systems. The substance was linked to neurodevelopmental disorders in children, including autism.
Even though the entire regulatory process spanned over seven years, once the ruling passed in January 2020, Member States had three months to dispose of all products containing chlorpyrifos.
“All pesticides are aimed at killing something,” Vijver explains. “If a substance is neurotoxic for insects, for example, that same neurotoxicity could apply to humans [...] Which is not so strange, because that’s the intention [of the pesticide].”
Denis Benoit, a former farmer in charge of pruning trees in the winter and applying pesticides from spring through summer, recalls going home with intense symptoms after a day’s work. “I had a fever at night and red patches on my arms,” he says. “It was because of the insecticides we were using, like D6.”
Like Nadan and Leduc, the 65-year-old from western France was also diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2019. “I do feel regret for having worked with those substances, but it was hard to find work at the time, and we were told they were only toxic in large doses,” he says.
‘Who sounds the alarm?’
For scientists like Vijver, the regular reassessment of pesticides is one of the few safeguards against such long-hidden harms, and it is precisely what the EU’s upcoming omnibus would remove.
Under the current EU system, a pesticide’s approval expires on a set date, and the company producing it has to show again that its product is safe to keep selling. If the approval no longer expires automatically, the product would stay on the market by default, removing the “safety lock” that Vijver refers to. The burden would then fall on the shoulders of regulators such as the EFSA or individual member states to sound the alarm.
“But who triggers the process? Doctors? Scientists? Or the guy who walks his dog and sees all the birds have died? That’s not our job,” says Vijver.
If passed, the legislation package would also increase the maximum grace period for farmers to substitute banned pesticides from 18 months to three years. Conditions for the exceptional use of banned pesticides, including endocrine disruptors, would also be loosened.
Sending a clear message of concern, Vijver took the initiative to write an open letter on September 17 and urged the European Parliament to pause the vote on the legislative package until an independent investigation into its potential health and environmental impacts is carried out. She gathered 573 other signatories from a wide range of disciplines, including environmental protection, medicine and public health – all of whom “have expertise” in the field, Vijver says.
“I’ve never done something like this before,” she admits. “As scientists, we are really worried. I would never have done this if I wasn’t really worried.”

The vote on Omnibus X is expected to take place at the end of October.
Victims take to the streets
Cancer victims and farmers marched arm in arm last weekend, flanked by doctors and activists, to protest pesticides. Organised by a handful of non-profits, the march saw 8,000 demonstrators gather outside a factory in northern France owned by Syngenta, the world’s largest pesticide seller.
Amid the crowd was Fleur Breteau, founder of the Cancer Colère collective, who made waves last year when she sparked a nationwide movement to block the reintroduction of the pesticide acetamiprid.
